justification:
Technical round 2 (re-check) for /csharp-dotnet/linq-deferred-execution/, focused on verifying the round-1 fix and doing a fresh pass for anything missed. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/csharp-dotnet/linq-deferred-execution.md` from Git Bash: PASS, blocks=22, executed=11, run twice back to back with identical output both times, including exact match on every wildcarded-timing block's non-timing numbers (17984 primes both runs, SLA/lookup counts exact and identical).

The round-1 blocking issue is fixed and independently re-verified against the primary source, not just re-read. I fetched Where.cs and Select.cs directly from raw.githubusercontent.com/dotnet/runtime/main (not the writer's cached claim) and read them line by line. Confirmed: the non-indexed `Enumerable.Where<TSource>(IEnumerable<TSource>, Func<TSource,bool>)` overload dispatches, depending on the runtime type of `source`, to `SizeOptIListWhereIterator<TSource>` (IList, size-optimized builds), `ArrayWhereIterator<TSource>`, `ListWhereIterator<TSource>`, or `IEnumerableWhereIterator<TSource>` - all `sealed partial class ... : Iterator<TSource>` with a hand-written `public override bool MoveNext()` using an explicit `_state` field (for the List/IEnumerable cases) or manual index arithmetic (for the array case). None of these classes, nor the `Where<TSource>(..., Func<TSource,bool>)` method itself, contains `yield return` anywhere - confirmed by grep across the whole file. The only `yield return` in Where.cs is inside the private `WhereIterator` method used exclusively by the separate indexed overload `Where<TSource>(IEnumerable<TSource>, Func<TSource,int,bool>)`. Select.cs has the identical shape: `ArraySelectIterator`, `ListSelectIterator`, `IListSelectIterator`, `IEnumerableSelectIterator` are all hand-written `MoveNext()` classes, and the sole `yield return` is in the private `SelectIterator` method backing the indexed `Func<TSource,int,TResult>` overload. This is exactly what the fixed paragraph (end of 'Writing Where and Select from scratch,' around line 357) now says: main overloads dispatch to hand-written iterator classes with explicit `MoveNext()`; only the indexed overloads fall back to a `yield return` iterator. The claim is accurate, not just plausible - I read the actual class bodies, not just class names. I also independently confirmed the MS Learn quotes the article attributes to `Enumerable.Where` and `Queryable.Where` are verbatim in the current live pages (fetched both directly): 'stores all the information that is required to perform the action' / 'is not executed until the object is enumerated' (Enumerable.Where remarks) and 'generates a MethodCallExpression ... passes the MethodCallExpression to the CreateQuery(Expression) method of the IQueryProvider' (Queryable.Where remarks, correctly paraphrased in the article as 'hands it to the source's IQueryProvider'). No misquotes found.

Fresh full re-read of the whole article (not just the fixed section) surfaced no new correctness problems: the double-enumeration arithmetic in both the opening example (4 + 4 = 8) and exercise 2 (Any 2 + foreach 3 + Count 3 = 8) still checks out by hand against the printed output; the streaming-vs-nonstreaming classification, the yield-return suspend/resume trace, the mine-vs-real interleaving comparison, and the IQueryable expression-tree inspection (no `.Compile()` or invocation anywhere in that block) are all still sound and unchanged from round 1's verified state. `ArrayWhereIterator.MoveNext()` in the real source does raw array indexing with a `(uint)index < (uint)source.Length` bound check instead of a `foreach`/enumerator, and `ListWhereIterator` calls `List<T>.GetEnumerator()` directly on the concrete struct enumerator rather than going through `IEnumerable<T>.GetEnumerator()` - both genuinely 'skip work a generic foreach can't' in the sense the article claims (avoiding interface dispatch on the list case, avoiding enumerator overhead on the array case), so that clause holds up too. I also noticed, without penalizing the article for omitting it, that the real Where/Select iterator classes additionally fuse consecutive `Where`/`Select` calls internally (e.g. `ArrayWhereIterator.Select` returns a fused `ArrayWhereSelectIterator` rather than nesting a generic iterator) - a nice detail the article doesn't need for its point.

Two issues from round 1 remain open and unaddressed on this branch, which is why the score is not yet at the 8.5 pass bar despite the blocking error being fixed: (1) the `System.Linq.EnumerableQuery<T>` claim in the IQueryable section ('its provider is .NET's own System.Linq.EnumerableQuery<T>, which compiles the tree back into a delegate and runs it in-process') is still uncited and the type is still absent from front matter `sources`, a Hard Rule 3 gap for a specific, non-obvious, correct-but-unsourced claim; (2) the Streaming bullet definition ('reads source elements one at a time and can yield a result element after reading just one') is still phrased as a general definition when Microsoft's own wording explicitly allows a streaming operator to consume more than one source element before yielding a result. Neither is a factual error (both are true as far as they go), so neither caps the score at 7 the way the fixed issue did, but rule 3 is a hard rule and a carried-over, previously-flagged gap keeps this a notch below 'only nits.'
